policy: Every item in this file is a DRAFT written without access to a scholarly reviewer. Status values: 'draft-unreviewed' (reasoned from the pinned WLC text and the pinned OSHB/BDB dataset) and 'needs-source-check' (a summary of a named historical source that has NOT been checked against an edition in this build). No item is labelled verified. Interpretation is never chosen for the reader: contested items list alternatives.

statusVocabulary.draft-unreviewed: Reasoned from the Hebrew text and pinned datasets; no human scholar has reviewed it.
statusVocabulary.needs-source-check: Summary of a named source; the source passage has not been verified in this build.

selections.rationale: ruach is in construct with Elohim and is the subject of a feminine participle (merachefet), matching ruach's usual feminine gender. The BDB outline lists 'spirit of God' and 'wind' as separate senses. Some interpreters read 'ruach Elohim' as the Spirit/breath of God; others read Elohim as an intensifier ('a mighty wind'). The Hebrew words alone do not settle between them.

citations.label: OSHB BDB entry t.bk.ab, senses 2 and 9
Discussed in standard commentaries on Gen 1:2 (e.g. E. A. Speiser, Genesis, Anchor Bible, 1964)

selections.rationale: ruach carries the first-person suffix ('my ruach'), speaking in the divine voice. The verb that follows (yadon) is itself of uncertain meaning, so the sense of ruach here depends on an unresolved verb.

citations.label: OSHB BDB entry t.bk.ab, senses 1 and 9

selections.rationale: Here ruach is the object of a causative verb of passing over the earth, in a sentence about the floodwaters subsiding; a natural wind is the reading the immediate clause supports. This does not exclude a theological reading of the cause.
ruach is qualified by 'qadim' (east) and 'azzah' (strong) and it moves the sea: a physical wind.
'ruach Elohim' is followed by wisdom, understanding and knowledge of craft; the construct with Elohim points to the divine-spirit sense. The text does not specify a mechanism.
nefesh chayah is used of sea creatures. It is the same phrase used later of the human in Gen 2:7, so it does not by itself mark humans off from animals.
'the human became a nefesh chayah' describes the human as a living being, in the same phrase used of animals in Gen 1:20. The text does not say the human 'has' a detachable soul.
nefesh is linked here with blood ('its nefesh, its blood') in the prohibition on eating blood; the verse itself equates the two. Life or vital principle fits the clause.
'the nefesh that they had made/acquired in Haran' counts people; nefesh stands for persons.
'if it is your nefesh' is an idiom of wish or will (compare English 'if it is your desire'); the BDB outline lists nefesh as the seat of appetite/desire.
The plural verb that follows ('let them have dominion') shows a collective referent: humankind, not a single male individual.

'ha-adam' carries the definite article and is formed from the 'adamah' in the same verse. Whether it means 'the human', 'the first man' or a generic 'earthling' before Eve appears is debated; the article shows it is not yet a personal name here.
'He called their name Adam' applies to male and female together ('their'), supporting the collective sense; the same word is used as a personal name elsewhere.
'dust from the adamah': the ground is named as the material of the human. The Hebrew has a sound link between ha-adam and ha-adamah (see the wordplay note).

citations.label: OSHB BDB entry a.bc.ac, senses 1 and 3

selections.rationale: 'cursed is the adamah because of you' is followed by labour and produce, so the ground as tilled and yielding sustenance is meant.
'all the families of the adamah' could mean the whole inhabited earth or the lands/territories of the world; the BDB outline lists both senses.
'the ground on which you stand is holy ground' refers to the physical surface under Moses' feet.
The verse has two occurrences with different senses: 'after these devarim' means 'these events/things' (matter, thing), while 'the davar of YHWH came' means a divine utterance.

citations.label: OSHB BDB entry d.ai.ab, senses II and IV

selections.rationale: 'Is any davar too wonderful for YHWH?' uses davar for a matter or thing, not a spoken word.

citations.label: OSHB BDB entry d.ai.ab, sense IV

selections.rationale: 'all these devarim' refers to spoken words/utterances the text then records.

citations.label: OSHB BDB entry d.ai.ab, senses II-III

selections.rationale: 'aseret ha-devarim' (the ten words) names the written utterances; the later label 'commandments' is not in this phrase.

citations.label: OSHB BDB entry d.ai.ab, sense III

selections.rationale: 'knowing good and evil' (yode'ei tov va-ra) is a participle phrase. Whether it means moral discernment, experiential knowledge or a comprehensive range ('everything') is debated; the verb alone does not decide it.

citations.label: OSHB BDB entry j.au.aa, Qal senses 1.1.a, 1.1.d, 1.1.e

selections.rationale: 'the man yada Eve his wife, and she conceived' uses the established idiom of marital intimacy; the following conception confirms the sense.
'who did not yada Joseph' can mean not being acquainted with him or not acknowledging him and his legacy; the text does not say which.

citations.label: OSHB BDB entry j.au.aa, senses 1.1.f and 1.2

selections.rationale: 'I know (yadati) their sufferings' is paired with 'I have seen' and 'I have heard'; knowledge by experience/awareness fits the cluster.

le-ovdah u-leshomrah pairs 'work' (avad) with 'keep/watch over' (shamar). The suffix -ah is feminine while gan (garden) is masculine in Hebrew, so grammatically the suffix more naturally points back to adamah (ground); interpreters differ on how to read the pairing.
cherubim and the flaming sword are placed 'to guard the way to the tree of life'; guard/keep-watch fits the purpose clause.
'Am I my brother's shomer?' uses the participle: keeper/one who has charge of.
'those who shamar my commandments': shamar with mitzvot means to observe/keep (obligations), a different sense from guarding a place.
'the Israelites shall shamar the Sabbath' is the observance sense the BDB outline lists separately as 'keep sabbath'.
avad with the ground as its object (le-ovdah) denotes working or tilling it.
'you serve me for nothing' - avad of working for another person, with a wages discussion in the same verse.

'you shall serve (ta'avdun) God on this mountain': avad with Elohim as object, the 'serve God' sense. The same verb appears for service to Pharaoh in the same book, which is part of the book's wordplay on service.
'six days you shall labour (ta'avod)' contrasts with the Sabbath rest: ordinary work.

tzelem ('image') is used with be- ('in/as'). What the 'image' consists of (bodily form, function as God's representative, relational capacities) is debated and is not defined in the verse. The same noun is used elsewhere of physical idols.
The verse repeats tzelem three times in a parallel structure ('in his image ... in the image of God he created him ... male and female he created them').
'in the image of God he made humankind' grounds the prohibition on shedding human blood; it reuses the Gen 1 language.

demut ('likeness') appears as ki-demutenu ('according to our likeness'). The BDB outline lists a sense of external appearance and an adverbial 'like as'; the relation between tzelem and demut (synonymous or qualifying) is debated.
'in the demut of God he made him' echoes Gen 1:26-27 before the genealogy; compare Gen 5:3 where Adam fathers a son 'in his demut, according to his tzelem'.

The servant prays 'show chesed to my master Abraham': a request for divine kindness. Chesed is a relational, loyalty-based act, not only an emotion. A separate lexical entry (chesed II, 'reproach', BDB lists it under separate numbering) is a different word and does not apply.

citations.label: OSHB BDB entry h.ed.ab, senses I.1 and II
Homonym note: see the lemma's 'distinct lexical entries' list

selections.rationale: 'doing chesed to thousands' predicates chesed of God toward those who love and keep his commandments; the covenantal, reciprocal setting is part of the sense.

citations.label: OSHB BDB entry h.ed.ab, sense II

selections.rationale: 'rav chesed ve-emet' is part of the divine self-description formula in the covenant-renewal narrative; the pairing with emet (faithfulness/truth) is a literary feature of the formula.

citations.label: OSHB BDB entry h.ed.ab, sense II

selections.rationale: 'whatever the human called it, that was its shem' - designation of animals.
'let us make a shem for ourselves' can mean reputation/renown, or a memorial. The construction 'make a name' is idiomatic; the narrative's concern with not being scattered is part of the context.

citations.label: OSHB BDB entry v.dv.ab, senses 2.b and 5

selections.rationale: 'this is my shem forever' - shem as the designation of God, in answer to Moses' question about the name in Exod 3:13.
'the shem of YHWH your God' designates God; what 'lifting up' the name 'in vain' (la-shav) prohibits (false oaths, empty invocation) is debated and is not decided by shem.

The dataset keeps olam as one undivided entry ('long duration, antiquity, futurity'). 'berit olam' is a covenant of long/lasting duration; the entry does not subdivide the sense, so no finer claim is made.
'El Olam' as a divine epithet: whether it means 'God of eternity', 'God of antiquity' or an older place-name tradition is discussed; the dataset does not decide.
le-olam is paralleled in the verse by le-dor dor ('to generation after generation'), indicating a long continuing duration.
le-olam of a servant who stays: the same word is understood differently in interpretive tradition (see the tradition note). The word alone does not require 'eternal' in every use.

nachash is the ordinary Hebrew word for serpent in the BDB outline. The verse itself calls it a creature of the field that YHWH God made; it does not name any other identity. Later identifications are interpretations, not lexical senses.
Moses' staff becomes a nachash: a snake, in a sign narrative.
'the staff that turned into a nachash': snake. (The related word tannin is used for the creature in Exod 7:9-12; the text uses two different words.)

The dataset glosses nefilim as 'giants'. The verse does not itself say 'giants': it says the nefilim were on the earth in those days, and that the 'mighty men of old' (gibborim) are linked to the passage. Proposed derivations (for example from the verb 'to fall') are proposals, not established meanings.

traditions.summary: Rashi reads bereshit as in a construct relationship ('in the beginning of God's creating') rather than as an absolute 'in the beginning'. The Hebrew allows both readings because of the vowel pointing's relation to the following verb.
traditions.check: Edition and page not verified in this build.

traditions.summary: Rashi comments on the 'ruach Elohim' that hovered over the water as the 'throne of glory' suspended in the air, an early rabbinic image he reports.
Rashi takes tzelem as 'mold/form' and demut as relating to understanding and discernment. This is his reading, not a lexical definition of the words.
Onkelos renders nefesh chayah in a way commonly translated 'a speaking spirit', stressing speech.
Rashi notes that animals are also called nefesh chayah, and says the human's is distinguished by added knowledge and speech.
Rashi links arum ('cunning') of the nachash with arumim ('naked') in Gen 2:25, a wordplay present in the Hebrew text itself.
The Greek translation renders nefilim with a word meaning 'giants' (gigantes). The LXX is not loaded in this edition, so this cannot be compared line by line here.
traditions.check: LXX text not part of this build; verify against Rahlfs or another critical edition.

traditions.summary: Targum Pseudo-Jonathan names two fallen angels, Shemhazai and Azael, in connection with the nefilim. This is a later expansive tradition, not a lexical meaning.
Rashi, following the rabbinic tradition, understands le-olam of the pierced servant as lasting until the Jubilee year rather than literally forever.

John 1:1 opens with 'In the beginning' and speaks of creation through the Word, widely recognised as echoing Gen 1:1-3. This is a Christian reading of the creation account, distinct from the Hebrew lexical meaning of reshit or davar.
The Greek translation of ehyeh asher ehyeh uses a participle meaning 'the one who is'; some Christian readings connect John's 'I am' sayings to this passage. These are later reception traditions.
traditions.check: LXX text not part of this build.

wordplay.text: ha-adam ('the human') and ha-adamah ('the ground') share the same consonants (אדם / אדמה) and are placed in one sentence: the human is formed from the ground. The text itself makes the connection by juxtaposition.
arum ('cunning/shrewd', of the nachash) closely follows arumim ('naked') in Gen 2:25 - the same consonants with a different sense; the narrative ties the two scenes by this echo.

Gen.1.headline: Creation account
literary: Repeated formulae structure the days: 'God said', 'and it was so', 'God saw that it was good', and the refrain 'there was evening and there was morning'.
Days 1-3 and 4-6 are often read as parallel (settings and then what fills them); this is a common observation about the structure, not a claim in the text.
context: The word bara ('created') is used in this chapter with God as its only subject.

debates.question: How is the first verse constructed?

views.view: Main clause: 'In the beginning God created'
views.attribution: traditional reading, reflected in most English translations

views.view: Dependent construction: 'When God began to create' / 'In the beginning of God's creating'

Gen.2.headline: The human, the garden and the first command
literary: Gen 2:4 introduces the first toledot ('generations/account') formula, which recurs in Genesis as a marker of narrative sections (the formula's occurrences can be found with the lemma index).
context: The ground (adamah), the human (adam) and tilling (avad) are tied together by sound and by the narrative.

views.attribution: grammatical observation (suffix is feminine; 'gan' is masculine)

Gen.3.headline: The nachash, the tree and the consequences
literary: The wordplay arum/arumim connects chapters 2 and 3.
The speakers' choice of the divine name changes in the dialogue (the serpent says 'Elohim', the narrator says 'YHWH Elohim'); this is an observable feature of the text.
context: The text does not identify the serpent with any figure other than a creature of the field; later identifications are interpretive traditions.

Gen.6.headline: Sons of God, daughters of men, nefilim
literary: Gen 6:1-4 is a short, compressed unit; its relation to the flood narrative is debated.
context: The Hebrew bene ha-elohim ('sons of God') appears in other biblical passages (e.g. Job 1:6).

Exod.3.headline: The burning bush and the divine name
literary: The name-revelation (3:13-15) turns on the verb hayah ('to be'); 'ehyeh' is first person singular imperfect.
context: 'ehyeh asher ehyeh' (3:14) is translated in several ways ('I am who I am', 'I will be what I will be', 'I will be who I will be'), because the imperfect can express present or future.

debates.question: How should 'ehyeh asher ehyeh' be translated?

views.view: I WILL BE WHAT I WILL BE

Exod.20.headline: The ten words
literary: The text calls them devarim ('words'), not 'commandments'; Exod 34:28 uses 'aseret ha-devarim'.
context: Verses are numbered the same in the Hebrew and English numbering for this chapter in the OSHB verse map.

debates.question: How are the ten words divided?

views.view: Various traditions divide the text into ten differently (including differing treatment of verses 2-6).
views.attribution: Jewish, Catholic/Lutheran and other Protestant traditions differ (summary; unchecked)
